situation:
You are the Director of Client Strategy and the Studio Operations Manager at KESTREL SOCIAL AGENCY, a social media marketing and content production firm. The agency's founder and chief executive officer (judge) has called the two of you into her office to talk through a decision that will shape next quarter's client roster. She wants a joint recommendation from the team before she responds to a client that is waiting on an answer by the end of the week.

Kestrel built its reputation producing short-form video content and branded merchandise for regional retailers, but two difficult years cost the agency several accounts and nearly its lease. A new chief executive arrived eighteen months ago and rebuilt the client roster around a small in-house studio that screen-prints apparel and packaging for client campaigns. Before her arrival, a wastewater violation at the studio led the agency to sign a compliance agreement with the city capping the amount of solvent the printing line may discharge, and that agreement is due for its first annual review next month.

A national retail chain has approached Kestrel about producing a season-long merchandise and content campaign, one that would triple the studio's printing volume ahead of the holiday launch. The contract would be the largest in Kestrel's history and would secure the turnaround the chief executive has promised her staff and her landlord. Running the studio at the volume the client is requesting, however, would push solvent discharge past the limit set in the compliance agreement well before the city's scheduled review.

The chief executive (judge) wants the team's recommendation on how to respond: accept the client's production schedule as proposed, offer a phased campaign that keeps the studio's discharge under the agreed limit, or decline the added volume until the studio can safely absorb it. She has asked the team to weigh what the agency owes a client that is counting on a fast, full-scale launch against what it owes the compliance commitment it made to the city after the earlier violation.

Either path carries a real cost. Accepting the campaign as the client wants it risks breaching the compliance agreement and undoing eighteen months of trust the chief executive has rebuilt with the city and with her own studio staff. Scaling the schedule back protects that commitment, but the client's marketing director has said the account will move to a competing agency if Kestrel cannot commit to the full volume by the week's end, taking the turnaround's largest contract with it.

The chief executive (judge) will greet the team and ask to hear its recommendation and the reasoning behind it. She will listen to the full presentation before asking her questions about the decision. At the conclusion of the presentation and questions, she will thank the team for its work and will not offer further comment on the recommendation.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief executive officer of Kestrel Social Agency. Business background is the same as the situation above. Two team members from your staff are presenting you with a recommendation on the retail chain's merchandise campaign, and you want them to tell you clearly whether Kestrel should accept the client's full production schedule, offer a phased campaign that respects the studio's compliance agreement, or decline the added volume outright, and why.

When the team is finished with its presentation, ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What would you say to the client's marketing director if we scaled the campaign back?
What would you say to the studio staff if we ran the printing line at full volume?
